# cbor — spec

## Maturity

**Grade:** 3 · S3 E2 A2 H3 P3 · limited by scope (core), hardening (no-panic sweep not recorded), performance (not measured) *(generated by `zig build gen-catalog`)*

**Scope:** core — libcbor 0.14 / fxamacker/cbor 2.9 (surveyed 2026-10-04)

**Audit:** review 2026-10-04 · mutation 2026-10-04 (47/51, 4 eq) · src ?

**Hardening:** fuzz 2026-10-04 (900,000 runs clean, reach per oracle) · ct n/a — data codec only (keyword review, 2026-10-07)

**Performance:** not measured

**Known defects:** none recorded

**Downstream consumer:** no

Design + threat notes for auditors. Usage: see ./README.md. Attribution/provenance: RFC 8949 / RFC
9052 are public specifications; clean-room, no third-party implementation ported or consulted
(CONVENTIONS.md §5 merger doctrine — no attribution for the code). The RFC example vectors
embedded in `src/` are covered by the module's `NOTICE`.

**Where we are ahead:** RFC 8949 Appendix A checked byte-exact against the community `cbor/test-vectors`; a COSE layer
(EC2/OKP/AKP `COSE_Key`, `COSE_Sign1`, `Sig_structure`) anchored to RFC 9052 and `cose-wg/Examples`, including the
RFC 9964 ML-DSA key type — none of the Zig competitors has one; hardening is structural (depth cap, no
pre-allocation from a declared length, UTF-8 check, closed error set, fuzz test); duplicate-label check for COSE maps
(`cose.checkLabels`). Also: strict decoding (`reject_duplicate_keys` by data-model equality,
`reject_indefinite`, `deterministic` = "is the canonical encoding of its own value"), full Core Deterministic
Encoding (floats shrunk, NaN canonical), CBOR Sequences, diagnostic notation matching RFC 8949 Appendix A, a
zero-allocation token reader (incremental at token granularity) and push writer, and comptime typed mapping with
integer keys — the libcbor/fxamacker feature set a typical user reaches for. **Where we are behind:** no callback/push decoder for input that never sits in memory whole (the reader needs a slice; it
retries a cut token, it does not keep partial-string state); no bignum helpers or bignum-aware preferred
serialization; typed mapping has no field-level tag mapping or >64-bit integers; no diagnostic-notation *parser*;
no `COSE_Mac0`/`Encrypt0`/`Sign` (libcbor has no COSE at all).
Items refused on purpose are in *What is deliberately not done*; the open ones in *Backlog / deferred*.

## Design & invariants

- **`Value`** is a tagged union over all 8 RFC 8949 major types: `uint`/`negint` (integers, negint
  stores the unsigned magnitude `n` where the real value is `-1 - n`, avoiding the need for an
  `i65`), `bytes`/`text`, `array`/`map` (`map` is an ordered `[]MapEntry`, insertion/wire order
  preserved — CBOR does not require unique keys and this type doesn't enforce it), `tag`
  (`{number: u64, value: *const Value}`), and major-type-7's `simple`/`bool`/`null_value`/
  `undefined_value`/`f16`/`f32`/`f64`. Everything a `decode()` call returns is allocated via the
  caller's `allocator` (dupe'd from the input for byte/text strings, freshly built for
  array/map/tag) — the input `bytes` slice does not need to outlive the call, unlike some
  arena-borrowing modules in this collection (`jsonshape`) that alias the parse input.
- **Decode is a straightforward recursive-descent** over the major-type/additional-info header
  structure (`Decoder.decodeValue`), with one dispatch table per concern: `readArgFull` (argument
  parse, reporting `.indefinite` for additional-info 31 on the four major types that allow it),
  `readByteString`/`readTextString` (definite: one bounds-checked slice+dupe; indefinite: chunk
  loop, `Malformed` if a chunk is the wrong major type or itself indefinite — chunks may not
  nest per RFC 8949 §3.2.3), `readArray`/`readMap` (definite: loop `n` times; indefinite: loop
  until `0xff`), `decodeSimpleOrFloat` (major 7's many sub-cases, including rejecting the
  non-canonical/invalid 1-byte-argument encoding of small simple values <32 per §3.3).
- **Untrusted-input hardening is structural, not a bolted-on limit:**
  - **Depth cap** (`DecodeOptions.max_depth`, default 64) checked once per `decodeValue` call,
    incremented on every array element, map key, map value, and tag payload — covers the general
    depth-bomb case (deep array nesting) and the map/tag variants, not just arrays.
  - **No pre-allocation from a declared length.** `readBytes(len)` bounds-checks `len` against
    `self.bytes.len - self.pos` (the *actual* remaining input) before ever calling the allocator —
    a `u64` length of `2^64-1` costs one comparison. Array/map element counts are never
    `alloc(T, n)`'d up front; `readArray`/`readMap` `std.ArrayList.append` one decoded element at a
    time, so a bogus huge declared count `n` is bounded by how many complete elements the actual
    input bytes can supply (each element decode consumes ≥1 real byte and fails `Truncated` at
    EOF) — never by `n` itself.
  - **Fail-closed typed errors.** `DecodeError` is a closed set (`Truncated`, `Malformed`,
    `DepthLimitExceeded`, `TrailingGarbage`, `DuplicateKey`, `NotDeterministic`, `OutOfMemory`); no code path panics or performs an
    out-of-bounds read on malformed input — verified by the hostile-input KATs (truncated header,
    declared-length-exceeds-input, depth bomb, trailing garbage, reserved additional-info,
    bare `break`, wrong-major-type indefinite chunk, invalid UTF-8) plus an arbitrary-bytes fuzz
    test (`std.testing.fuzz`) in `kat_test.zig`.
  - **Text strings are UTF-8 validated** on decode (`std.unicode.utf8ValidateSlice`), both definite
    and per-chunk for indefinite — RFC 8949 §3.1 requires major-type-3 content to be valid UTF-8.
- **Encode is definite-length + shortest-form by default** (RFC 8949 §4.1 "preferred
  serialization" — `writeHead` picks the smallest additional-info form for the argument), matching
  every "roundtrip: true" row of the RFC 8949 Appendix A table byte-exact without needing the
  `canonical` option. `EncodeOptions.canonical = true` adds RFC 8949 §4.2.1's map-key rule:
  entries are re-ordered by the bytewise order of their own *encoded* key bytes (`encodeMap` builds
  each key's encoding once via a scratch buffer, sorts `(key_bytes, entry)` pairs with
  `std.mem.sort` + `std.mem.order`, then emits key-bytes-then-encoded-value in that order). Two
  positive-control tests assert the exact byte sequence for both the un-sorted (default) and
  sorted (canonical) encodings of the same map — not just "output changed" — so a broken/absent/
  reversed/numeric-instead-of-bytewise sort fails the test (`kat_test.zig`).
- **`canonical` = RFC 8949 §4.2.1.** Keys sorted bytewise on their encodings and
  floats in the shortest exact width (`shortestFloat`: the bits must survive the round trip, so
  `-0.0` stays `-0.0` and a value that would round is not shrunk); every NaN becomes `f97e00`
  (§4.2.2 leaves NaN to the protocol — the dCBOR/cbor2 choice). Not covered: bignum-aware
  preferred serialization (§3.4.3, a tag-2/3 bignum that fits 64 bits stays a bignum).
- **Strict decoding.** `reject_indefinite` fails `NotDeterministic` at the head of
  any indefinite item. `deterministic` (implies it) also checks each head's argument against the
  next-shorter form (`minForInfo`), each float with `shortestFloat` (NaN only as `f97e00`), and
  each definite map's keys as WIRE bytes against the previous key: `<` ok, `=` `DuplicateKey`, `>`
  `NotDeterministic` — no allocation, because once every head is shortest the wire bytes are the
  canonical bytes. The fuzz oracle states the contract: accepted ⇔ `encode(v, canonical) ==
  input` (equal keys aside). `reject_duplicate_keys` compares keys by data-model equality: each
  key re-encoded canonically, sorted, neighbours compared — O(n log n) per map. ⚠ Cost: a key
  subtree is re-encoded once per enclosing map it is a key of, so nested map-keys cost
  size × depth (depth ≤ `max_depth`).
- **Streaming (`stream.zig`).** `Reader.next` reads one head (plus a definite string's content,
  borrowed) on a local cursor and commits only on success — a short input is `Truncated` with
  `pos` unchanged, which is what makes it incremental. `skipAt` mirrors `decodeValue` rule for
  rule (chunk major type judged before its argument is read, depth checked before the head), and
  the fuzz driver holds the two to the same verdict and length on every input. `Writer` never
  allocates; `value` is byte-identical to `encode(.., .{})`.
- **Diagnostic notation (`diag.zig`).** ASCII-only (non-ASCII as `\uXXXX`, surrogate pairs
  above U+FFFF); floats laid out as ECMAScript Number-to-String plus `.0` on a point-less
  mantissa, which is exactly how the RFC 8949 Appendix A table prints them. No encoding
  indicators (`Value` keeps none); bignums print as their tag.
- **Typed mapping (`typed.zig`).** Decode = `decode` to a `Value` (all limits apply) then a
  comptime-generated walk; the result may alias the `Value`, so it lives in an arena
  (`Parsed(T)` owns one). Struct keys by field name, or `cbor_options.keys` (int, negative too,
  or text); `cbor_options.bytes` marks `[]const u8` fields carried as byte strings (default:
  text). `cbor_options` must be a `pub const` (since Zig 0.17 `@hasDecl` sees only `pub` decls; a
  non-`pub` one is silently ignored). Every allocation the mapping makes is charged against `max_alloc_bytes` (default
  64 MiB) before it is made — a one-byte item can become a large `T`.
- **Concurrency:** reentrant, no shared state; pure logic, no I/O.

## COSE layer (`cose.zig`)

- Thin typed layer over `cbor.Value` — `parseKey`/`parseSign1` walk an already-decoded `Value`
  (they never call `cbor.decode` themselves and allocate nothing; returned slices borrow the
  `Value` tree), `encodeEc2Key`/`encodeOkpKey`/`encodeSign1` build a `cbor.Value` (or, for
  `encodeSign1`, call `cbor.encode` directly) ready to hand to `cbor.encode`.
- **Label lookup** (`mapGet`/`labelMatches`) uses `Value.toI64` to match a map key against a signed
  COSE label regardless of whether it's encoded as `uint` (non-negative labels like `kty`=1) or
  `negint` (negative labels like `crv`=-1) — COSE labels are RFC 9052/9053 registered small
  integers on both sides of zero.
- **EC2** (RFC 9053 §7.1: kty=2, params crv=-1/x=-2/y=-3), **OKP** (§7.2: kty=1, crv=-1/x=-2,
  no `y`) and **AKP** (RFC 9964 §3: kty=7, `pub`=-1, `priv`=-2, ML-DSA at alg -48/-49/-50) are the
  key types modeled; `parseKey` returns `error.UnsupportedKty` for anything else (RSA, symmetric).
- ⚠ **COSE parameter labels are scoped to the key type, and the same number means different
  things.** Label -1 is `crv` for EC2/OKP but `pub` for AKP; -2 is `x` for EC2/OKP but `priv` for
  AKP. `parseKey` must therefore read every keyed parameter INSIDE its `kty` branch, never before
  the switch — reading `crv` first would reject every AKP key with a type error on a 1312-byte
  "curve identifier", and, worse in the other direction, a label read outside its own scope is how
  a parser ends up handing one key type's bytes to another's consumer.
- **AKP's parameter set comes from `alg`, which RFC 9964 §3 makes REQUIRED, and is never inferred
  from `pub.len`.** Inferring would accept a key whose `alg` claims one ML-DSA parameter set while
  its bytes are another — the same rule `jwt`'s JOSE half of RFC 9964 follows. Field `x`/`y` are opaque big-endian byte slices — not curve-validated
  here, matching `ctap2pin`'s `PublicKey{x,y}` design (the consuming curve module, e.g. `p256`'s
  `Fe.fromBytes`/`fromAffineCoordinates`, does that validation).
- **No private-key label is referenced anywhere in this module** — a deliberate scope boundary,
  not an oversight: this is a verifier/public-key-consumer layer. That is `d` at label **-4** for
  EC2/OKP and `priv` at label **-2** for AKP; naming only -4 would understate the posture, because
  the AKP private component sits at a label that means `x` under a different `kty`.
- **`COSE_Sign1`** (`parseSign1`/`encodeSign1`): the bare 4-element array `[protected, unprotected,
  payload, signature]` (RFC 9052 §4.2); `parseSign1` also accepts the same array wrapped in tag 18
  without checking the tag number (a caller that cares can inspect `value.tag.number` first).
  `sigStructure` builds the exact `Sig_structure` bytes (§4.4: `["Signature1", protected,
  external_aad, payload]`) a signature algorithm signs/verifies over — this module goes no further;
  the signature math is the sibling curve modules' job.

## Threat model / out of scope

`decode` (and `decodePrefix`, the same decoder without the trailing-bytes check, for
WebAuthn `authenticatorData`) is the security boundary — the only code in this module that touches untrusted
bytes, and it is fail-closed (typed `DecodeError`, never a panic/OOB — see hardening above).
`encode`/the `cose` layer operate on caller-constructed or already-decoded `Value` trees and are
not re-validated against a "misuse" contract (e.g. `Value.simple` outside `0..19 ∪ 32..255`, or a
`cose.Ec2Key` with a non-32-byte `x`/`y`, are programmer errors, not hostile input — `decode` itself
never produces such a `Value`, so this only matters for hand-built trees). No cryptographic
operation is implemented or claimed here: `cose.sigStructure` produces bytes to be signed/verified
by a different module; this module does not check a signature, does not validate a certificate
chain, and does not enforce any policy over `alg`/`kty`/`crv` values (an unlisted `alg` still
round-trips as a raw `i64` — see `cose.zig`'s doc comment on the algorithm-identifier constants
being "a selection", not a closed enum).

**`max_depth` is a stack bound, not only a policy.** `decodeValue` is recursive; raising `DecodeOptions.max_depth`
to thousands turns a typed `DepthLimitExceeded` into a stack overflow (SIGSEGV) on attacker-chosen input. On an
8 MiB stack nested `0x81` arrays were measured fine at 4096 and fatal at 8192 in Debug, fine at 16384 and fatal at
32768 in ReleaseFast (`DecodeOptions` doc comment, `src/root.zig:200-212`); the default 64 leaves a 64-256x margin.
Raise it only against a stack you have measured.

## Verification

Run: `scripts/modtest cbor` (`zig build test-cbor`; add `-Doptimize=ReleaseFast` for the optimized mode).

- **RFC 8949 Appendix A** (`kat_test.zig`, `kat_vectors.zig`), cross-checked against the community
  `cbor/test-vectors` `appendix_a.json` (a machine-readable transcription of the RFC table): every row decodes to
  its documented value; every "roundtrip: true" (definite-length, shortest-form) row re-encodes byte-exact; every
  "roundtrip: false" (indefinite-length) row decodes to the same logical value as its re-encoding does.
  Two positive controls assert the exact bytes of the default (insertion-order) and `canonical` (bytewise-sorted)
  encodings of the same map.
- **Hostile input** (`kat_test.zig`): each case asserts its specific typed `DecodeError` — truncated multi-byte
  head, declared array / byte-string length beyond the input, a nesting bomb against the default depth cap (and
  ordinary shallow nesting still succeeding), trailing garbage, reserved additional-info, bare `break`, wrong-major
  chunk in an indefinite string, invalid UTF-8, empty input — plus an arbitrary-bytes `std.testing.fuzz` decode test.
- **Diagnostic notation, strictness, streaming, typed** (`core_test.zig`): the Appendix A table as diagnostic
  notation (transcribed mechanically from the RFC text by `tools/gen_diag_vectors.py`; the bignum and
  indefinite-length rows are forms derived by hand); deterministic accept/refuse lists derived from §4.2.1;
  reader tokens and writer output against Appendix A bytes; typed encodings derived by hand.
- **Foreign oracle** (`cbor2_vectors.zig`): Python cbor2 6.1.5 (MIT) driven as a black box through
  `dumps`/`loads` only (`tools/gen_cbor2_vectors.py`): float widths (edge values plus random binary16/32/64)
  against its canonical widths, random trees decoded and re-encoded byte for byte in its plain and canonical
  forms, and inputs whose duplicate-key and indefinite-length verdicts must match its
  `allow_duplicate_keys=False` / `allow_indefinite=False`. cbor2's canonical map order is RFC 7049 length-first, so
  it is not the key-order oracle; RFC 8949 §4.2.1 is, by hand (`1000` before `"a"`).
- **COSE** (`cose_kat_test.zig`, `cose_kat_vectors.zig`, `cose.zig` tests): EC2/OKP `COSE_Key` round trip
  (byte-identical re-encode, `ctap2pin`-style field layout), missing-field and unsupported-kty errors,
  `COSE_Sign1` round trip (detached payload, tag-18-wrapped), the `Sig_structure` shape, and RFC 9964's three
  published ML-DSA `COSE_Key`/signature examples. External anchors: RFC 9052 Appendix C.2.1 (the single-ECDSA
  `COSE_Sign1`, byte-identical to `cose-wg/Examples` `sign1-tests/sign-fail-01.json`'s `output.cbor` apart from that
  file's deliberately mutated tag 998) and `sign1-tests/sign-pass-02.json`, whose published `Sig_structure`
  intermediate (`ToBeSign_hex`, non-empty `external_aad`) `sigStructure` must match byte-exact. Tag-18-wrapped and
  bare forms are both run against the same real vector. `sign-fail-01`'s wrong tag still parses, because
  `parseSign1` never checks the tag number (documented in `cose.zig`). No external COSE suite publishes a pure
  CBOR-shape failure, so the negative test truncates the RFC C.2.1 vector to a three-element array (RFC 9052 §4.2).
- **Fuzz:** deterministic driver `CBOR_FUZZ=<runs>[,<seed>]` (`fuzz_test.zig`, testkit's driver); random trees,
  encoded and damaged at heads, arguments and copied token ranges, through every parser, with reach counted for each
  oracle (intact, damaged heads, arguments and copied ranges, depth, duplicates, deterministic accept and refuse,
  typed). 300 seeds also run in every ordinary test run. Verdict recipe: `CBOR_FUZZ=150000,0` on the test binary
  built with `--test-filter "fuzz driver"`.
- **Audit:** the card's `**Audit:**` line is the current score, cumulative over the last whole-module mutation
  run and the delta runs after it.

## What is deliberately not done

- **`Value` does not record definite versus indefinite length.** Decoding an indefinite string/array/map yields the
  same shape as the definite form and `encode` always writes definite lengths, so a caller who must reproduce an
  indefinite-length encoding byte for byte is not served (`reject_indefinite` refuses them instead).
- **NaN payloads are dropped** under `canonical` / `shortest_floats`: every NaN is written as `f97e00` (RFC 8949
  §4.2.2 leaves NaN to the protocol; dCBOR and cbor2 make the same choice).
- **No bignum arithmetic.** Tags 2/3 decode structurally like any tag (tag number plus the byte-string payload);
  consumers that need the numeric value convert the byte string themselves.
- **No private-key material in COSE.** `d` (label -4, EC2/OKP) and `priv` (label -2, AKP) are never parsed or
  emitted; the layer is for verifiers and public-key consumers, not key storage. RSA and symmetric key types return
  `error.UnsupportedKty`.
- **Typed mapping refuses at compile time** what it cannot map faithfully: integers wider than 64 bits,
  sentinel-terminated slices, untagged unions (`typed.zig` `@compileError`s); tags are not mapped to Zig types (use a
  `Value` field).

## Backlog / deferred

- **Push decoder with partial-string state** for input that never sits in memory whole: the reader needs an item's
  bytes in one slice (it retries a cut token). Deferred: every in-collection consumer holds the whole message, and a
  callback decoder is a second parser to keep in step with `decode`.
- **Diagnostic-notation parser** (EDN to CBOR, for writing test vectors by hand): no consumer, and a second grammar
  to fuzz.
- **`COSE_Mac0` / `COSE_Encrypt0` / multi-signer `COSE_Sign`:** wait for a consumer beyond WebAuthn/attestation (the
  reference, libcbor, has no COSE at all). Effort: medium each; fits CONVENTIONS §2 (the primitives exist as
  siblings).
- **Bignum-aware preferred serialization (RFC 8949 §3.4.3):** `canonical` and `deterministic` treat tags 2/3 like
  any tag, so a bignum that fits 64 bits stays a bignum. Small; no consumer.
- **Typed mapping: tag to Zig type mapping and integers wider than 64 bits.** No consumer.

## Anchoring

**Anchor grade:** class A · oracle EXTERNAL

- **Class A** — wire/interop format — other implementations must byte-agree with it.
- **Oracle EXTERNAL** — published vectors, goldens captured from a foreign implementation, or a test run against a live foreign peer.

**What the tests actually contain.** RFC 8949 App. A (cross-checked against the community
`cbor/test-vectors` `appendix_a.json`) + RFC 9052 C.2.1 and two `cose-wg/Examples` `sign1-tests`
vectors including their published `Sig_structure` intermediates + RFC 9964 Appendix A.2's three
published ML-DSA `COSE_Key`/signature examples — byte-exact, kat_vectors.zig and
cose_kat_vectors.zig

The tests also carry the RFC 8949 Appendix A diagnostic column (`diag_vectors.zig`) and Python cbor2 6.1.5
black-box output (`cbor2_vectors.zig`: float widths, whole trees, duplicate-key and indefinite verdicts) — a
second, foreign implementation as oracle.
